title: Packed rows walked through unaligned loads and counted stores
surface: unalign_reg_for_load / unalign_reg_for_store state, ub_cursor, ub_to_reg_unalign_pre / ub_to_reg_unalign / reg_to_ub_unalign / reg_to_ub_unalign_post for the streaming path, and ub_to_reg_unalign_once / reg_to_ub_unalign_once for the stateless one
study_for: Two spellings of the same walk, and what separates them. The streaming path carries state: one `unalign_reg_for_load` and one `unalign_reg_for_store`, a `ub_cursor` per row, a prime before the row's first chunk and a `reg_to_ub_unalign_post` that closes the row's store chain. The stateless path carries none: each chunk names its own element offset and nothing is remembered between them. Both are run over all six geometries, and both must produce the same bytes.

The source allocation is deliberately larger than the payload. `capacity = ((cells + 64 + 7) // 8) * 8` adds a full register of slack past the data and rounds the end up, which is what makes a full-register load legal when the last chunk of a row is partial. The destination has no slack at all -- it is exactly `cells` -- so every store passes an explicit `count` that has to stay inside the row. Read those two allocations together; copying one without the other is how this kind of walk goes wrong.

Only row 0 is necessarily aligned. With no padding between rows, row `i` starts at element `i * width`, so the byte phase of a row depends on the width: the 3x64 geometry has every row aligned (the control), while 5x17 and 4x33 put almost every row at a different phase. Having both in the matrix is what makes a pass mean something -- an implementation that only handled the aligned case would fail eleven of the twelve cases rather than looking fine.

The body adds the row index and nothing else. That is a diagnostic decision: every cell of row `i` differs from the input by exactly `i`, so a cell that came from the wrong row is off by the difference of two row numbers, and the failure output prints those offsets. A body that computed something interesting would make the same addressing mistake much harder to read.
do_not_copy_when: You are about to give the destination the source's slack, or the source the destination's exactness. The asymmetry is the point: reads may overrun into slack, writes may not overrun at all.

You are treating a green model run as proof that the final store-chain flush is optional. It is not. `reg_to_ub_unalign_post` closes the chain, and a CPU check cannot establish the vendor hardware's buffering behaviour when it is left out -- that question needs a card.

You are reusing the streaming state across rows. The cursor and the load state are primed per row here. Carrying either into the next row leaves the previous row's phase in it, and nothing in the API stops you.

Your rows are padded to a register boundary. Then none of this is needed -- an ordinary aligned load and store per row is both simpler and faster, and the geometry that proves it is `3x64`, the one case here where the unaligned path has nothing to correct.
